Walk me through one ML application that: Pick one specific project and structure it as: what the model did (business purpose), the handoff from data science (artifact format, evaluation report), what you built for serving/deployment, and how you monitored it in production - concrete specifics at each stage make this credible versus a generic lifecycle description.
Have you built any FastAPI services?: Answer with a specific example if yes - what the service did, why FastAPI was chosen (async support, automatic OpenAPI docs, type validation via Pydantic), and its scale/traffic characteristics - specificity here sets up credible follow-up depth.
Can you describe one FastAPI service you: Name the service's purpose, its endpoints and their responsibilities, how it handled validation/errors, and how it was deployed (containerized on GKE/Cloud Run) and monitored - a concrete walkthrough beats a generic 'I built a REST API' description.
What endpoints did you expose?: List the actual endpoints and their purpose (e.g. a `/predict` endpoint for inference, a `/health` endpoint for readiness checks, a `/metrics` endpoint for Prometheus scraping) - grounding this in the real API surface of a project you've worked on.
Why did you design multiple endpoints in: Separate concerns by responsibility - a health/readiness endpoint shouldn't share logic with the actual inference endpoint (so Kubernetes probes don't accidentally trigger expensive model calls), and splitting by resource/action (predict, batch-predict, model-info) keeps each endpoint's request/response schema focused and independently versionable rather than one overloaded endpoint handling everything via request-body branching.
How was the overall API designed?: Describe the resource/endpoint structure, request/response schemas (typically Pydantic models in FastAPI, giving automatic validation and OpenAPI docs), versioning approach (URL path versioning like /v1/predict), and error handling convention (consistent error response shape, proper HTTP status codes) - showing deliberate API design decisions rather than an ad hoc set of routes.
How did you authenticate and authorize u: Common approaches: API key validation via a FastAPI dependency checking a header against a stored key/hash, OAuth2/JWT bearer tokens validated on each request (FastAPI's built-in OAuth2PasswordBearer scheme), or, for internal service-to-service calls, mTLS or a service mesh handling identity - the choice depends on whether callers are external clients or internal services.
How did you ensure only authorized users: Layer authentication (verifying who's calling) with authorization (verifying what they're allowed to do) - e.g. validating a JWT's signature and expiry, then checking claims/roles within it against the specific action being requested, implemented as a reusable FastAPI dependency applied to every protected route rather than duplicated per-endpoint logic.
Where have you used MLflow?: Answer with actual scope - experiment tracking (logging params/metrics/artifacts during training) versus also using the Model Registry for versioning and stage transitions, and whether you operated the tracking server infrastructure yourself or used a managed/shared instance.
How did you use MLflow in your project?: Describe the concrete workflow - logging training runs (parameters, metrics, the model artifact itself) via the MLflow SDK during training, comparing runs in the MLflow UI to select the best candidate, and registering the chosen model version in the Model Registry for downstream deployment.
Was model versioning required?: If yes, explain why - typically because multiple model versions needed to coexist (a production version and a candidate being evaluated), or because rollback capability was a hard requirement given the model's business criticality - grounding the 'yes' in a concrete reason rather than a bare confirmation.
How did you implement model versioning?: Each trained model gets registered in the MLflow Model Registry as a new version under a named model, with metadata linking it to the training run, data snapshot, and evaluation metrics - the serving layer references a specific registered version (or a stage alias like 'Production') rather than always pulling 'whatever was trained most recently.'
How did rollback work using MLflow?: Since each version remains in the registry indefinitely, rollback is reassigning the 'Production' stage/alias back to the previous version (a fast, low-risk registry operation) and redeploying the serving layer to load that version - no retraining or data recovery needed, since the prior artifact was never deleted.
Which LLMs have you worked with?: Name the specific models and the context each was used in (e.g. a cloud-hosted model for a RAG application, an open-weight model self-hosted for cost/control reasons) - specificity about actual usage context is more convincing than a list of model names alone.

Have you worked with Terraform or Ansibl: Answer with actual scope for each - Terraform for provisioning cloud infrastructure (which resource types, how modules were structured) versus Ansible for configuration management/application-level automation on existing servers - these solve different problems and the distinction matters for the follow-up.
Walk me through what you've built using: Name specific infrastructure provisioned (VPCs, GKE clusters, IAM bindings, Cloud SQL instances), how modules were organized, and how state was managed (remote backend, environment separation) - concrete resource types and a real module design decision demonstrate genuine hands-on Terraform experience.
How have you used Ansible?: Describe specific playbooks/roles built - configuration management on VMs (package installation, config file templating), or orchestrating a multi-step deployment sequence - Ansible is typically used for the configuration/application layer that Terraform (which provisions infrastructure) doesn't handle.
How do Terraform and Ansible work togeth: A common pattern: Terraform provisions the infrastructure (VMs, networks, load balancers), and Ansible then configures the software/application layer on top of that provisioned infrastructure (installing packages, deploying application code, managing configuration files) - Terraform's local-exec or an external CI step often triggers the Ansible run against the newly created hosts once Terraform finishes provisioning them.
Imagine multiple ML teams need self-serv: Provide a shared platform layer (a standardized training pipeline template, a model registry, a common serving framework) that teams self-serve through a simple interface (a CLI, a Terraform module, or an internal developer portal) rather than each team building their own infrastructure from scratch - the platform team owns the underlying infra/guardrails while ML teams focus on models, with clear self-service boundaries (what they can configure themselves) versus what requires platform team involvement.
How would you provide isolation between: Separate GCP projects or Kubernetes namespaces per team with ResourceQuotas, distinct IAM/service accounts scoped to only that team's resources, and separate model registry namespaces/prefixes - so one team's training job or model can't consume another's compute quota or accidentally overwrite another's model version.
How would you allow different teams to m: Give teams self-service control over their own pipeline configuration and deployment cadence within guardrails (they can deploy whenever they want, but must pass the same automated evaluation/security gates), rather than a centralized platform team being a bottleneck approving every team's every change - the platform provides paved-road defaults, not a mandatory single release train everyone must follow together.
How would you handle governance and secu: Enforce non-negotiable guardrails centrally (mandatory evaluation gates before production promotion, required vulnerability scanning, least-privilege IAM templates every team must use) while leaving team-specific decisions (which model architecture, which training schedule) to the teams themselves - governance should be built into the paved-road platform itself (so compliant usage is the easy path) rather than enforced through manual review of every team's actions.
How would you design observability for s: A shared observability layer teams get automatically by using the platform - standardized metrics emitted by the common serving framework (latency, error rate, prediction/confidence distribution) flowing into a shared Grafana/Cloud Monitoring setup, plus a shared drift-detection pipeline teams configure with their own thresholds - so teams get production-grade monitoring by default rather than each building it themselves inconsistently.
From an ML inference service perspective: Latency (p50/p95/p99) and error rate as the baseline service-health signals, plus model-specific signals - prediction/confidence distribution, input feature drift, and accuracy/F1 once ground truth becomes available - since a model can be fast and error-free while quietly returning degraded predictions, which only the model-specific metrics would catch.

How did you identify cost optimization o: Start from the billing console's cost breakdown by service/project/label to find the largest cost centers, cross-reference with utilization metrics (are provisioned resources actually being used, e.g. low-utilization VMs, over-provisioned node pools, unattached persistent disks) to find waste specifically, rather than guessing at savings opportunities without data.

If starting a new ML project today, woul: Give a reasoned answer based on team context rather than a universal preference - Vertex AI for faster time-to-production with less operational overhead when the team doesn't need deep customization or wants to avoid running Kubeflow/MLflow infrastructure themselves; Kubernetes-based open-source tooling when avoiding vendor lock-in, needing multi-cloud portability, or requiring customization Vertex AI doesn't support is a hard requirement.
Why would you choose one over the other?: The deciding factors are usually: team size and platform engineering capacity (open-source tooling needs someone to operate it), how much customization the ML workflow genuinely needs beyond what a managed platform supports, cost model fit (managed platforms trade operational simplicity for a different pricing structure), and organizational cloud strategy (multi-cloud/portability requirements push toward open-source).
What are the trade-offs between Vertex A: Vertex AI: faster to get started, less operational burden, tightly integrated with other GCP services, but less customizable and ties you to GCP. Kubernetes-based (Kubeflow, MLflow, KServe): fully customizable and cloud-portable, but requires a team to build and operate the platform itself, which is real ongoing engineering investment that a smaller team may not be able to sustain.
